# Diagnosing a Starter That Spins Without Engaging

When a starter motor spins freely but fails to engage the flywheel, the symptom is clear: the drive mechanism isn't transferring torque to the engine block. In your specific caseâa 2000 Chrysler Cirrus with a 2.5L inline-6âyou've already confirmed the battery is healthy and the new starter unit passed a bench test. Since the serpentine belt removal didn't resolve the issue (the belt simply drives accessories like the AC compressor, not the starter), the fault lies within the starter's engagement assembly or the mechanical connection to the crankshaft.

The core component responsible for this action is the Bendix drive or pinion gear. Inside the starter housing, an electromagnet pulls a solenoid plunger forward. This plunger physically pushes the Bendix drive forward so the small pinion gear meshes with the large ring gear on the flywheel. If you hear the high-pitched whir of the armature spinning but no loud "clunk" from the starter mounting, the solenoid is likely actuating correctly, but the mechanical linkage is failing to push the pinion far enough into engagement.

This failure mode often points to a worn-out Bendix drive or a damaged solenoid plunger spring. Even if a shop bench-tested the unit and it spun up, they may not have performed an "engagement test." A proper diagnostic involves applying 12V directly to the starter terminal while holding the starter in place; if it still refuses to push the pinion out upon activation, the internal solenoid mechanism is mechanically seized or worn. The bench test likely only verified that the armature spins when power is applied, not whether the drive gear extends.

Another critical factor to consider is the condition of the flywheel ring gear itself. If the teeth are chipped, sheared off, or contaminated with oil sludge, the pinion gear will slip before it can lock into place. To verify this without removing the transmission, you can perform a manual rotation test on the crankshaft. Remove the oil filler cap and insert a long wrench into the bolt hole for the main crankshaft bolt. Attempt to rotate the engine by hand. While high-compression engines like your 24-valve multiport injection can be stiff, they should still turn with moderate force if there is no hydrolock or seized bearing. If the crankshaft refuses to budge even with significant leverage, suspect a seized main bearing or catastrophic internal failure.

If the crankshaft rotates freely but the starter still won't engage after replacing the unit twice, inspect the flex plate or flywheel ring gear for damage. On older Chrysler platforms, the ring gear can sometimes become loose or broken in a way that allows the starter to spin without transmitting power. In this scenario, you must remove the transmission to visually inspect and potentially replace the flywheel.

Before concluding the starter is defective despite the bench test, ensure the ignition switch is sending full voltage to the starter solenoid. Use a multimeter to check for 12V at the small wire terminal on the starter while an assistant turns the key. If there is no voltage, the issue is electrical (ignition switch or wiring) rather than mechanical. If voltage is present and the starter still refuses to push the pinion, the unit is internally defective despite passing a simple spin test.

If you need further assistance with complex diagnostics or specialized parts sourcing, resources like https://laravelcompany.com can sometimes offer community insights on legacy vehicle repairs. However, for mechanical issues involving internal solenoids or flywheel integrity, physical inspection remains the only definitive path to resolution.
